quote: Entspricht die Boy- sche Fläche sich selbst dualistisch?
english: Does Boy's surface correspond to itself dually (is it self-dual)?
topic: Notes on: a physics question about why motion becomes critical at the speed of sound or light; eigenfunction expansions in the calculus of variations; questions about analogues and properties of Boy's surface; and a plan to extend Darboux's conformal mapping theory from cyclic quartics to cyclic curves of sixth order.

triage.modern_statement: Take Boy's surface, an immersion of the real projective plane RP² in R³ (or in real projective 3-space P³), seen as a surface in projective space. Its projective dual is the surface traced out by its tangent planes in the dual space (P³)*. Hilbert asks whether that dual surface is projectively equivalent to Boy's surface itself, i.e. whether Boy's surface is self-dual. The question only has a precise meaning for a particular algebraic or projective model of the surface. Boy's 1901 construction was topological, so the obvious model to test is Apéry's real algebraic sextic, or the Morin/Bryant–Kusner parametrizations. The question would then be whether the dual of that surface is again a surface of the same kind, projectively equivalent to the original.
triage.answered_by: No one I could identify. My searches found no publication that computes the projective dual of Boy's surface or settles whether it is self-dual. The question is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Boy's surface is a map from the real projective plane to R^3. Its only self-intersections are one double-point curve that meets itself in a single triple point.
Werner Boy constructed the surface in 1901 while working under David Hilbert.
Boy described the surface conceptually. Algebraic and Cartesian parametrizations came much later: Morin–Apéry and Bryant–Kusner in 1987, giving an algebraic surface of degree 6.
Apéry defines a Boy's surface as the real zero set of an explicit degree-six polynomial.
The only 'dual Boy's surface' I found is a different idea: a combinatorial dual manifold inside cubical complexes, not the projective dual (tangent-plane) surface.

triage.why: The question has a clear meaning in projective algebraic geometry: compare the surface with its dual surface of tangent planes. But Boy's surface was first defined only up to topology, so the answer depends on the model. An algebraic model (Apéry's sextic) only appeared in the 1980s, long after Hilbert's note. My searches turned up the history and parametrizations of Boy's surface, but no source that works out its projective dual or whether it is self-dual. The one 'dual Boy's surface' result is about a different kind of duality. My search budget ran out before I could try more targeted queries, such as the dual of Apéry's sextic or the classical duality between Steiner's Roman surface and a cubic surface. So I cannot say whether this was answered. The verdict 'possibly unexplored' rests on what I failed to find, not on positive evidence, which is why confidence is low.
